analysis.one_liner: Rewards companies that move jobs back to America and taxes companies that move them offshore.
analysis.headline: The Senate failed 53-45 on a vote that needed 60 to even begin debating the bill, with every Republican present voting no.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given companies a two-year holiday from employer payroll taxes for each worker they hired in the United States to replace an offshore worker. It would have stripped tax deductions and credits from the costs of shutting down a US operation to open one abroad, and it would have ended the ability of US multinationals to defer American tax on profits from goods made offshore and imported back into the country. The Senate never got to debate it: a procedural vote to start consideration won a majority but fell short of the 60 votes needed, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: American workers, especially in industries where jobs are commonly moved offshore, such as manufacturing, back-office services, and call centers. The payroll tax holiday rewards employers who bring those jobs back with US-based hires, and the two penalty provisions change the tax math that currently favors moving work abroad. The Medicare and Social Security trust funds are explicitly held harmless — the general fund repays any revenue the payroll holiday costs them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: American workers whose jobs move offshore

how_it_helps.text: Exempts employers from payroll taxes for 24 months on wages paid to a US-based hire who replaces an offshore worker, reducing the cost of onshoring a job by roughly the employer's 6.2% share of payroll taxes.

Denies any tax deduction, loss, or credit for costs incurred in an 'American jobs offshoring transaction' — shutting down or shrinking a US operation in connection with starting or expanding that business abroad — while carving out severance, outplacement, and retraining costs for displaced US workers.

Ends the deferral of US tax on income of a controlled foreign corporation attributable to goods produced by jobs moved offshore and then imported into the United States, so those profits can no longer be kept out of US taxation indefinitely.
Transfers general-fund money to the Social Security and disability trust funds equal to the revenue the payroll holiday forgives, so worker-benefit financing is not depleted.

analysis.who_pays: US multinational corporations. Firms that offshore jobs would lose deductions for the cost of the move and would pay current US tax on profits from offshore-made goods imported back into the country. The general Treasury bears the cost of the payroll tax holiday.

drawbacks.text: The payroll holiday is narrow: an employer must certify by sworn affidavit that a specific new US worker replaces a specific offshore worker who was not a citizen or lawful resident, and only one hire counts per replaced employee, limiting how many firms could actually use it.

Denying deductions and taxing imported-property income would raise the tax bill for US-based multinationals across the board, and critics argue such penalties raise companies' costs without guaranteeing any jobs actually return.

Repealing deferral on offshore manufacturing income can complicate foreign tax credits and invites the standard objection that it puts US multinationals at a disadvantage against foreign competitors in foreign markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly attacked the tax code's tilt toward moving jobs abroad, but its main hiring incentive was so narrowly drawn — one certified replacement hire per offshore position — that its job-creating reach may have been modest, and the new corporate taxes carry real compliance complexity and competitiveness objections. The penalty provisions were the more durable part; the payroll holiday would have cost the Treasury money for uncertain gains.

outcome.mechanism: A Senate procedural vote to open debate on the bill won a majority, 53 to 45, but needed 60, so the bill never came to the floor and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on September 21, 2010 with eight cosponsors — seven Democrats and the chamber's one independent — and it was placed on the Senate calendar the next day.
A cloture motion on the motion to proceed was presented on September 24, the first step in forcing debate on a bill in the Senate.

On September 28, 2010, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 53-45, falling seven votes short of the 60 required; 52 of 57 voting Democrats backed it and all 40 Republicans present, plus the one independent, opposed it.

Because the Senate could not even start debating the bill, no committee consideration, floor debate, amendment process, or final vote ever occurred, and the bill expired with the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshoring multinationals, which keep their deductions for moving jobs abroad and keep deferring US tax on profits from offshore-made goods imported into the country; workers whose jobs depend on those tax breaks stayed exposed.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost perfectly by party: 52 of 57 voting Democrats backed opening debate while every one of the 40 Republicans present voted no, joined by the chamber's single independent; four Democrats also defected, leaving the motion seven votes short of the 60 needed.

industries.industry: US multinational corporations that offshore jobs
industries.note: These firms would lose tax deductions for the cost of moving US operations abroad and would owe current US tax on profits from offshore-made goods imported back into the US — the two provisions aimed squarely at the tax advantages of offshoring. Their interest in keeping those breaks runs against workers whose positions move overseas.

industries.industry: Offshoring and outsourcing service providers (IT, call centers, back-office)
industries.note: The deduction denial covers the business lines and contract arrangements built on shifting US work abroad, shrinking the market for outsourced offshore delivery of services consumed in the US.
A company that brings an offshore job back to a US-based worker gets 24 months free of employer payroll taxes on that hire, directly subsidizing domestic employment.
